grammar.title: Ser: who you are, and 'I' can go
explain: With the verb ser you say who or what you are, and where you're from: soy Claire, soy de Holanda, Augusto es de Lima.
In Spanish you usually leave out 'yo' (I). The verb ending already tells you who does it: soy = I am, hablo = I speak, vivo = I live.
grammar.compare: English: I am, you are, he is. Spanish: (yo) soy, (tú) eres, (él/ella) es. Where English always needs 'I', Spanish just says 'soy'. 'Yo soy' isn't wrong, but it sounds like you're stressing it: 'I am (not him)'.

examples.en: Are you Peruvian? No, I'm Dutch.

exercises.why: Where you're from goes with ser: soy de…
Hablo = I speak. No need for 'yo'.

1.goal_en: Tell the driver your name, which country you're from and which city you live in.

2.title_en: What you need: el or la?

ex.w1-41: The bathroom is at the back, on the right.
ex.w1-42: A coffee with milk for me, please.

grammar.title: Tener or estar, and el or la
explain: Hungry, thirsty, cold or hot: in Spanish you 'have' them, with tener. Tengo hambre (I have hunger), tengo sed, tengo frío.
How you feel (tired, sick, happy) goes with estar: estoy cansada, estoy enferma. As a woman you end in -a: cansada, enferma. Augusto says cansado.
Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine. Masculine: el / un (el vaso, un café). Feminine: la / una (la carta, una mesa). Words ending in -o are usually masculine, in -a usually feminine.
grammar.compare: English says 'I am hungry, I am cold'. Spanish says 'I have hunger, I have cold': tengo hambre, tengo frío. And where English has just 'the' and 'a', Spanish has el/la and un/una. Watch out: agua is feminine, but you say 'el agua' because it sounds better. So: el agua está fría.

examples.es: La mesa, el vaso, una servilleta, un café.
examples.en: The table, the glass, a napkin, a coffee.

exercises.why: Agua is feminine (fría), but you say 'el agua'.

2.goal_en: Order still water and ask where the bathroom is.

grammar.title: Tú or usted?
explain: Tú and usted both mean 'you'. Tú is informal, usted is polite. In Peru you say usted a lot: to older people, strangers, taxi drivers and waiters, and often to your partner's parents and uncles.
With tú the verb usually ends in -s: ¿cómo estás?, ¿de dónde eres?, ¿puedes…? With usted you use the same form as for he or she, without -s: ¿cómo está?, ¿de dónde es?, ¿puede…?
grammar.compare: English has only one 'you' and shows politeness with words like 'sir' or 'could you'. Spanish shows it in the verb: ¿puedes? (friendly) or ¿puede? (polite). If in doubt in Peru, choose usted: it's always polite. To Silvia you say tú; to uncle Diego you say usted, until he says 'tutéame' (call me tú).

exercises.why: Silvia is young and family: tú, so eres.
Strangers and people serving you get usted.

3.goal_en: Speak to uncle Diego with usted and to cousin Silvia with tú, at least 3 sentences to each.

grammar.title: Numbers, and 'tener' for your age
explain: In Spanish you 'have' your age, with tener: tengo veinticinco años = I have twenty-five years. So never 'soy veinticinco'.
16 to 29 are written as one word: dieciséis, veintidós, veinticinco. From 31 on with 'y' (and): treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco. A hundred is cien.
Peruvian mobile numbers have 9 digits and start with a 9. You say them digit by digit or in groups of three.
grammar.compare: English: I'm twenty-five. Spanish: tengo veinticinco años (I have twenty-five years). The good news: the order is the same as in English, tens first: forty-five = cuarenta y cinco (forty and five).

exercises.why: Tens first, then 'y', then the units.

exercises.q: Put the words in the right order

4.goal_en: Say how old you are, ask Silvia how old she is and give her your 9-digit mobile number.
